nodes.label: Nation-state Author
nodes.notes: Operation Olympic Games (publicly attributed). Objective: sabotage enrichment without overt kinetic action.

nodes.label: Stuxnet
nodes.notes: ~500KB worm. Four zero-days, two stolen code-signing certs, first known PLC rootkit. Highly targeted: only acts on a specific Siemens S7 config.

nodes.label: Contractor Laptop
nodes.notes: Patient zero on the IT side — vendor/contractor machine.

nodes.label: Engineering PC
nodes.notes: Windows host. Worm spreads via USB autorun, network shares, and the print-spooler flaw (MS10-061).

nodes.label: WinCC SCADA DB
nodes.notes: Siemens WinCC with hard-coded default DB credentials — a propagation vector.

nodes.label: STEP7 / WinCC Eng. WS
nodes.notes: Siemens engineering station. Stuxnet infects STEP7 project files and hijacks s7otbxdx.dll to intercept PLC comms.

nodes.label: Siemens S7-300 PLC
nodes.notes: Rogue ladder logic injected. First-ever PLC rootkit: hides its own code from the engineer.

nodes.label: IR-1 Centrifuge Cascade
nodes.notes: Rotor speed driven out of tolerance (nominal ~1064 Hz pushed toward 1410 Hz, then 2 Hz). Cumulative mechanical damage over months.

nodes.label: Operator HMI / SCADA
nodes.notes: Operators shown pre-recorded 'all normal' values — the sabotage is masked in real time.

nodes.label: Insider courier
nodes.notes: Reported (2019 Yahoo News / de Volkskrant investigation) to be an engineer recruited by Dutch intelligence who physically introduced Stuxnet on removable media. Earlier theory: unwitting contractors carried it in. Either way a human had to cross the air gap — there was no network path.

nodes.label: Global spread · AV discovery 2010
nodes.notes: An aggressive 2010 variant spread far beyond Natanz once an infected laptop reconnected to the internet. VirusBlokAda then Symantec analysed it mid-2010 — the first cyber-physical weapon became public.

edges.label: infected laptop taken out, plugged in online
